definitions.definition: An educated guess that you test with experiments.
definitions.example: Like saying 'plants grow faster with music' and then testing it.

definitions.definition: The tendency to look for evidence that supports what you already believe and ignore evidence that doesn't.
definitions.example: If you think a certain sports team is the best, you only notice their wins and forget their losses.

definitions.definition: When an idea or statement proves itself wrong.
definitions.example: Saying 'I never tell the truth' is self-refuting because if it's true, it's a lie.

definitions.definition: An endless chain of causes or reasons where each step depends on the previous one, never reaching a starting point.
definitions.example: If you say 'I know it because my friend said so, and my friend knows it because another friend said so...' and it never ends.

definitions.definition: When an idea disagrees with what we observe in the real world through experiments or measurements.
definitions.example: Claiming 'water freezes at 100°C' is an empirical contradiction because we see it freeze at 0°C.

definitions.definition: When parts of an idea contradict each other, making it impossible for the whole thing to be true.
definitions.example: Saying 'I am both 10 years old and 20 years old at the same time' is logically incoherent.

definitions.definition: When an idea cannot explain something it is supposed to explain.
definitions.example: A theory of gravity that can't explain why apples fall is an explanatory failure.

definitions.definition: Einstein's theory that gravity is caused by mass bending space and time, like a heavy ball on a trampoline.
definitions.example: It explains why planets orbit the sun and why light bends around stars.

definitions.definition: Ripples in space-time that spread out when massive objects, like black holes, crash into each other.
definitions.example: Like ripples in a pond when you throw a rock, but in the fabric of space itself.

definitions.definition: Points in space-time where gravity is so strong that the normal laws of physics break down, like the center of a black hole.
definitions.example: Imagine a point where matter is crushed to infinite density, and time stops.

definitions.definition: The idea that being in a gravitational field feels exactly the same as accelerating in a spaceship.
definitions.example: If you're in an elevator with no windows, you can't tell if you're being pulled by gravity or pushed upward by a rocket.

definitions.definition: A basic truth that is accepted without proof, used as a starting point for other reasoning.
definitions.example: In math, 'the shortest distance between two points is a straight line' is an axiom.

definitions.definition: Something that is true but has no explanation for why it is true; it just is.
definitions.example: The fact that the universe exists might be a brute fact—there's no reason behind it.

definitions.definition: When an argument uses its conclusion as one of its premises, going in a circle without proving anything.
definitions.example: Saying 'the Bible is true because it says it's true' is circular.

definitions.definition: A type of math that studies curved surfaces and spaces, like the surface of a sphere or the shape of the universe.
definitions.example: It's the math used to describe how space bends around a planet.

definitions.definition: In math, a space that looks flat and smooth when you zoom in, like the surface of the Earth seems flat when you stand on it.
definitions.example: A donut's surface is a smooth manifold—it's curved but has no sharp edges.

definitions.definition: The law that the total amount of energy and momentum in the universe stays the same; it can't be created or destroyed.
definitions.example: When you throw a ball, the energy from your arm goes into the ball's motion—nothing is lost.

definitions.definition: The slow, gradual shift in the orbit of Mercury around the sun, which was a mystery until Einstein's theory explained it.
definitions.example: Like a spinning top that wobbles as it spins, Mercury's orbit slowly rotates over time.

definitions.definition: The shortest path between two points on a curved surface, like the path an airplane takes on a globe.
definitions.example: A straight line on a flat map is not a geodesic on Earth—planes fly curved paths to save fuel.

definitions.definition: When two different things have the same structure or pattern, even if they look different on the surface.
definitions.example: A map of a subway system and a family tree can be isomorphic if they have the same connections.

definitions.definition: A way for computers to find patterns in complex data by assuming the data lies on a curved surface.
definitions.example: It's how a computer can recognize faces by finding the 'curved space' of facial features.

definitions.definition: A branch of math that uses curved spaces to measure how much information data gives about an unknown quantity.
definitions.example: It helps scientists design experiments to get the most information from the fewest measurements.

definitions.definition: When two systems have the same underlying connections and rules, even if they are about different things.
definitions.example: A computer's circuit and a city's road network can be structurally isomorphic if they have the same layout.
